claim: Populations of Drosophila melanogaster were exposed to repeated seasonal changes in resources across 58 generations.
source: Here we exposed populations of Drosophila melanogaster to repeated seasonal changes in resources across 58 generations and used experimental and mathematical approaches to investigate how viability selection on body size in the non-breeding season could affect demography.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the experimental design involving 58 generations of D. melanogaster populations.

claim: Opposing seasonal episodes of natural selection on body size interacted with both direct and delayed density dependence to cause populations to undergo predictable multigenerational density cycles.
source: We show that opposing seasonal episodes of natural selection on body size interacted with both direct and delayed density dependence to cause populations to undergo predictable multigenerational density cycles.
evidence: This is the main finding stated in the abstract, supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Seasonality can set the conditions for life-history trade-offs and density dependence, which can interact to cause multigenerational population cycles.
source: Our results provide evidence that seasonality can set the conditions for life-history trade-offs and density dependence, which can, in turn, interact to cause multigenerational population cycles.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental results presented in the study.

claim: Sequential episodes of reproduction and survival caused by seasonality could be a major source of fluctuations in the strength and direction of natural selection.
source: Consequently, sequential episodes of reproduction and survival caused by seasonality could be a major source of fluctuations in the strength and direction of natural selection (Darwin, 1859; Lack, 1954; Fretwell, 1972; Schluter et al., 1991; Bell, 2010; Bergland et al., 2014), giving rise to classic life-history trade-offs (Lack, 1947; Roff, 1992; Stearns, 1992; Garland, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Traits that confer a fecundity advantage but are associated with a survival cost will experience natural selection in one season that is opposed by selection in the subsequent season.
source: More specifically, traits that confer a fecundity advantage, but which are associated with a survival cost, will experience natural selection in one season that is opposed by selection in the subsequent season (Levins, 1968; Michod, 2006; Bell, 2010; Bergland et al., 2014).
evidence: This theoretical concept is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Large individuals usually have higher fecundity.
source: Large individuals usually have higher fecundity (Mueller and Joshi, 2000; Schulte-Hostedde and Millar, 2004), but they could also have lower survival during the non-breeding season when resources are scarce (Stockhoff, 1991; Reznick et al., 2000; Munch et al., 2003; Monaghan, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Large individuals could have lower survival during the non-breeding season when resources are scarce.
source: Large individuals usually have higher fecundity (Mueller and Joshi, 2000; Schulte-Hostedde and Millar, 2004), but they could also have lower survival during the non-breeding season when resources are scarce (Stockhoff, 1991; Reznick et al., 2000; Munch et al., 2003; Monaghan, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Large individuals might take more time to grow and require more resources for maintenance.
source: In addition, large individuals might take more time to grow and require more resources for maintenance (Munch et al., 2003), which could negatively impact their survival probability (Kingsolver and Huey, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Populations of D. melanogaster do not show evidence of multigenerational cycles when kept under aseasonal conditions.
source: In addition, populations of D. melanogaster do not show evidence of multigenerational cycles (Mueller and Joshi, 2000), even when kept under the same conditions as our breeding season (i.e. 'aseasonal populations'; Appendix 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and reference to an appendix with additional data.

claim: 45 replicate populations were submitted to the seasonal treatment and tracked for 58 generations in the long-term control experiment.
source: In the first experiment, we submitted 45 replicate populations to the seasonal treatment described above and tracked the total number of individuals and body size at the end of the breeding and non-breeding season for 58 generations (the 'long-term control' treatment; Figure 1).
evidence: The experimental design is explicitly described in the text and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: 13 additional populations were tracked over 31 generations in the 'stop-selection' treatment where viability selection was experimentally prevented.
source: In the second experiment, we tested the role of viability selection during the non-breeding season by tracking 13 additional populations over 31 generations using a similar protocol to the 'long-term control', but in which we experimentally prevented viability selection in the 'non-breeding' season by providing high levels of food during this season (the 'stop-selection' treatment; Figure 1).
evidence: The experimental design is explicitly described in the text and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: 13 replicate populations were tracked over 31 generations in the 'short-term control' experiment using the same protocol as the 'long-term control'.
source: This 'short-term control' experiment also had 13 replicate populations tracked over 31 generations (Figure 1).
evidence: The experimental design is explicitly described in the text and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: The 45 replicated seasonal populations showed a predictable increase in abundance during the breeding season and a decline in the subsequent non-breeding season over 58 generations.
source: Over 58 generations, the 45 replicated seasonal populations showed a predictable increase in abundance during the breeding season, where the food medium allowed females to lay eggs, and a decline in the subsequent non-breeding season (Figure 2a), as is typical of many natural seasonal systems.
evidence: This observation is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Short seasonal cycles were embedded within longer multigenerational cycles where average population size fluctuated 3-fold.
source: However, the autocorrelation functions (ACF) also revealed that these short, seasonal cycles were embedded within longer multigenerational cycles where average population size fluctuated 3-fold (insert in Figure 2a).
evidence: This finding is based on autocorrelation function analysis of the population data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The ACF function was characterized by stationary periodic dynamics, which resulted in an oscillatory decay to zero.
source: In these populations, the ACF function was characterized by stationary periodic dynamics, which resulted in an oscillatory decay to zero (Figure 2a inset).
evidence: This is a description of the autocorrelation function pattern observed in the data.

claim: There is a negative correlation between population size at the end of the non-breeding season and body size at the end of the non-breeding season (Pearson's product-moment correlation = −0.64; t = −4.48, p<0.001).
source: As expected, there is a negative correlation between population size at the end of the non-breeding season and body size at the end of the non-breeding season (Pearson's product-moment correlation = −0.64; t = −4.48, p<0.001), suggesting that density negatively impact body size in the non-breeding season.
evidence: This statistical result is explicitly stated with test statistics.

claim: Mean survival during the non-breeding season was 71% (±0.21 SD).
source: Mean survival during the non-breeding season was 71% (±0.21 SD) and survival was density-dependent (βsurvival = −0.001, t = −27.73, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the experimental data.

claim: Survival during the non-breeding season was density-dependent (βsurvival = −0.001, t = −27.73, p<0.001).
source: Mean survival during the non-breeding season was 71% (±0.21 SD) and survival was density-dependent (βsurvival = −0.001, t = −27.73, p<0.001).
evidence: This statistical result demonstrates density-dependent survival.

claim: Mean female dry weight was significantly lower after the non-breeding season (0.279 mg) than before the non-breeding season (0.381 mg).
source: Mean female dry weight was significantly lower after the non-breeding season (0.279 mg, n = 3620 females) than before the non-breeding season (0.381 mg; n = 5258 females; standardized values = 0.577 before and −0.566 after the non-breeding season; Welch t-test: t = −35.90, df = 1,589.240.24, p<0.001; Figure 2b)
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the experimental data with statistical support.

claim: Viability selection on body size was density-dependent in the long-term control.
source: and this viability selection was density-dependent (Figure 2c; Table 1, Appendix 3).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in Figure 2c and Table 1.

claim: When population size was high at the start of the non-breeding season, there was stronger selection for smaller flies.
source: That is, when population size was high at the start of the non-breeding season, there was stronger selection for smaller flies and this was driven by changes in mean dry weight after the non-breeding season rather than changes in the mean dry weight before the non-breeding season (Appendix 3).
evidence: This interpretation is based on the analysis of body size data across different densities.

claim: Average dry weight measured after the non-breeding season showed multigenerational cycles.
source: Average dry weight measured after the non-breeding season also showed multigenerational cycles (Figure 2d), as indicated by the autocorrelation function (Figure 2d, inset), varying between average peaks of 0.32 mg and lows of 0.23 mg.
evidence: This finding is based on autocorrelation function analysis of body size data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: There was no evidence of multigenerational population cycles in the 'stop selection' populations.
source: Unlike the 'long-term controls' (Figure 2a), there was no evidence of multigenerational population cycles in these 'stop selection' populations (Figure 3a inset).
evidence: This observation is based on autocorrelation function analysis shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Body size did not significantly decline after the non-breeding season in the 'stop selection' treatment.
source: In addition, body size did not significantly decline after the non-breeding season (Figure 3b; average body size was 0.337 mg before and 0.331 after the non-breeding season; n = 1290 and n = 689 females, respectively; standardized values: 0.028 before and −0.052, respectively; Welch t-test: t = −1.733, df = 1,479.400.40, p=0.081).
evidence: This statistical result shows no significant change in body size.

claim: There was no evidence of density-dependent selection in the 'stop selection' treatment.
source: There was also no evidence of density-dependent selection (Figure 3c; Table 1) and no evidence of cycles in body size (Figure 3d inset).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in Figure 3c and Table 1.

claim: The 'short-term control' exhibited evidence for multigenerational cycles over 31 generations.
source: Over 31 generations, and similar to the 'long-term control' (Figure 2a), the 'short-term control' exhibited evidence for multigenerational cycles (Figure 4a).
evidence: This observation is based on data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Female dry weight significantly decreased from an average of 0.371 mg before the non-breeding season to 0.276 mg after the non-breeding season in the 'short-term control'.
source: Overall, female dry weight significantly decreased from an average of 0.371 mg before the non-breeding season (n = 968 females) to 0.276 mg after the non-breeding season (n = 623 females; standardized values = 0.487 before and −0.761 after the non-breeding season; Welch t-test: t = −30.601, p<0.001; Figure 4b)
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the experimental data with statistical support.

claim: The magnitude of viability selection was stronger when densities were higher at the start of the non-breeding season in the 'short-term control'.
source: but the magnitude of this viability selection was stronger when densities were higher at the start of the non-breeding season (Table 1, Figure 4c).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in Table 1 and Figure 4c.

claim: In the 'long-term control' and 'short-term control', fecundity and survival were influenced by density in the current and past season.
source: In the 'long-term control' and 'short-term control', fecundity and survival were influenced by density in the current and past season (Table 2 and Table 3).
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical models shown in Tables 2 and 3.

claim: The 'stop-selection' experiment showed evidence of delayed effects on fecundity but not on survival.
source: In contrast, the 'stop-selection' experiment showed evidence of the delayed effects on fecundity (Table 2), but not on survival (Table 3), meaning that the 'stop-selection' treatment eliminated both viability selection on body size as well as delayed effects of density on survival.
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical models shown in Tables 2 and 3.

claim: A mathematical model including delayed density dependence and viability selection resulted in multigenerational cycles in population size.
source: A mathematical model including delayed density dependence as well as the effects of body size on survival (viability selection) and fecundity resulted in multigenerational cycles in population size (before red line in Figure 5a), similar to those observed in our 'long-term control' and 'short-term control' (Figure 2a and Figure 4a, respectively).
evidence: This is a result from the mathematical model shown in Figure 5a.

claim: The model without viability selection on body size and delayed density dependence resulted in the elimination of multigenerational cycles.
source: The model without viability selection on body size and delayed density dependence (i.e. including only effects of current abundance on fecundity and survival), resulted in the elimination of multigenerational cycles (after red line in Figure 5a), as observed in our 'stop selection' populations (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is a result from the mathematical model shown in Figure 5a.

claim: The exclusion of only viability selection led to unstable population dynamics where the population crashed after 10 generations.
source: The exclusion of only viability selection eliminated the fitness trade-off in body size and allowed larger flies to survive to breed. This led to unstable population dynamics (i.e. the population crashed after 10 generations; Figure 5b) because larger flies have greater fecundity and there was a negative interaction between body size and abundance.
evidence: This is a result from the mathematical model shown in Figure 5b.

claim: The exclusion of delayed density dependence alone eliminated the cycles.
source: The exclusion of delayed density dependence alone eliminated the cycles (Figure 5c), suggesting that viability selection and delayed density dependence are necessary for these persistent multigenerational cycles to occur.
evidence: This is a result from the mathematical model shown in Figure 5c.

claim: The model with low heritability (h2 = 10−5) also generated multigenerational population cycles.
source: The model with low heritability (h2 = 10−5) also generated multigenerational population cycles (Figure 5d).
evidence: This is a result from the mathematical model shown in Figure 5d.

claim: The interplay between density-dependence and evolutionary trade-offs caused by seasonality can have important consequences for population dynamics.
source: Our results provide empirical and mathematical evidence that the interplay between density-dependence and evolutionary trade-offs caused by seasonality can have important consequences for population dynamics.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined experimental and modeling results.

claim: Seasonal variation in resources resulted in a fitness trade-off and multigenerational population cycles in the experimental system.
source: In our experimental system, seasonal variation in resources resulted in a fitness trade-off and multigenerational population cycles.
evidence: This is a summary of the main experimental finding.

claim: Population cycles were observed in the absence of predation, long-term fluctuations in resources, or any explicit negative-frequency dependence.
source: These cycles were observed in the absence of predation, long-term fluctuations in resources, or any explicit negative-frequency dependence, all of which are known to cause regular fluctuations in population size (Lindström et al., 2001; Yan et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement describes the experimental conditions and contrasts them with other known causes of population cycles.

claim: The evolutionary response to selection might not be required to observe feedback between ecological and evolutionary processes, as long as selection is strong.
source: Our results suggest that the evolutionary response to selection might not be required to observe feedback between ecological and evolutionary processes, as long as selection is strong.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results, particularly from the low heritability model.

claim: In flies, body size is highly heritable.
source: In flies, as in many other species, body size is highly heritable (Prout and Barker, 1989), and it is reasonable to suppose that, in our populations, offspring from smaller flies tend to be smaller.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Strong selection can affect trait distributions within generations even when genetic variation is low.
source: However, even when genetic variation is low, strong selection can still affect trait distributions within generations (Grafen, 1988), potentially affecting population size.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Selection for body size during the non-breeding season was strong enough to drive observed cycles, potentially in the absence of any genetic change across generations.
source: In our experimental system, selection for body size during the non-breeding season was strong enough to drive observed cycles, potentially in the absence of any genetic change across generations.
evidence: This interpretation is based on the experimental results and modeling with low heritability.

claim: Simulations with the mathematical model with essentially zero heritability (h2 = 10−5) generated multigenerational population cycles.
source: Simulations with our mathematical model with essentially zero heritability (h2 = 10−5 as opposed to 0.3) also generated multigenerational population cycles because viability selection changed the distribution of body size, which subsequently affected fecundity.
evidence: This is a result from the mathematical model.

claim: Long-lasting effects of past density on survival were essential to generate the multigenerational cycles according to the mathematical model.
source: We showed that variation in non-breeding abundance can cause density-dependent selection, but our mathematical model suggested that long-lasting effects of past density on survival were essential to generate the multigenerational cycles.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the mathematical modeling results.

claim: Competition during the non-breeding season can negatively impact the physiological conditions of the survivors, reducing their breeding output in the following breeding season.
source: We have shown how competition during the non-breeding season can negatively impact the physiological conditions of the survivors, reducing their breeding output in the following breeding season (Ratikainen et al., 2008; Betini et al., 2013a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: Delayed density dependence alone would cause short cycles and population crashes after only a few generations according to the mathematical model.
source: Our mathematical model also suggested that the delayed density dependence alone would cause short cycles and population crashes after only a few generations.
evidence: This is a result from the mathematical modeling.

claim: The addition of viability selection allowed for sustained multigenerational cycles according to the model.
source: It is clear from the model that the addition of viability selection allowed for sustained multigenerational cycles, as was observed in our empirical results.
evidence: This is a conclusion from comparing different versions of the mathematical model.

claim: In a predator-prey system, evolutionary changes in the prey population extended density cycles compared to the typical quarter-period phase lags between prey and predator densities.
source: For example, in a predator-prey system, evolutionary changes in the prey population extended density cycles compared to the typical quarter-period phase lags between prey and predator densities (Yoshida et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Evolutionary effects on population cycles are now believed to be widespread in lab systems.
source: This evolutionary effect is now believed to be widespread in lab systems (Becks et al., 2012; Hiltunen et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Opposing viability and fecundity selection on body size was necessary for the persistence of multigenerational population cycles.
source: Opposing viability and fecundity selection on body size was necessary for the persistence of multigenerational population cycles.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental and modeling results.

claim: Fitness trade-offs between seasons are likely more common than currently appreciated.
source: Such fitness trade-offs between seasons are likely more common than currently appreciated (Schluter et al., 1991; Schmidt et al., 2005; Schmidt and Conde, 2006, Schmidt and Paaby 2008; Kingsolver and Diamond, 2011; Behrman et al., 2015), especially given that many organisms use vastly different habitats over the annual cycle.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Sexually selected traits enhance mating success but might also reduce survival during the non-breeding season.
source: For example, sexually selected traits enhance mating success, but might also reduce survival during the non-breeding season (Emlen, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Increased development rates can accelerate age of first reproduction but are often associated with reduced survival during the adult stage.
source: Alternatively, increased development rates can accelerate age of first reproduction, but are often associated with reduced survival during the adult stage (Stearns, 1992; Kingsolver and Huey, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Seasonal fitness trade-offs represent a form of balancing selection, which can maintain increased levels of genetic variation at evolutionary equilibrium.
source: Seasonal fitness trade-offs also represent a form of balancing selection, which can maintain increased levels of genetic variation at evolutionary equilibrium (Barton and Keightley, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Seasonal fluctuations in selection might allow for the maintenance of increased adaptive potential in populations.
source: Seasonal fluctuations in selection might allow for the maintenance of increased adaptive potential in populations (Shaw and Shaw, 2014), facilitating more rapid responses to directional environmental change (Bradshaw and Holzapfel, 2006; Bell, 2010; Huang et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Examples of delayed density dependence causing cycles have been documented in natural populations subjected to strong seasonality.
source: Examples of delayed density dependence causing cycles have been documented in natural populations subjected to strong seasonality (Merritt et al., 2001; Stenseth et al., 2003; Yan et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: During the breeding season, adults were placed in vials with a dead yeast-sugar medium to lay for 24 hr.
source: During the breeding season, we placed adults in vials (28 × 95 mm) with a dead yeast-sugar medium to lay for 24 hr (day 0), after which adults were discarded and larvae were allowed to mature to adults (16 days).
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol.

claim: The non-breeding season consisted of an empty vial with food provided by a pipette tip filled with 0.200 ml of 5% water–sugar solution per day.
source: The non-breeding season consisted of an empty vial of the same size as the breeding vials, but food was provided by a pipette tip filled with 0.200 ml of 5% water–sugar solution per day from the top of the vial.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol.

claim: The water-sugar solution was sufficient for many flies to survive (~95% survival at low population size) but did not allow females to lay eggs.
source: This solution was sufficient for many flies to survive (~95% survival at low population size) but did not allow females to lay eggs (Bownes and Blair, 1986; Betini et al., 2013a).
evidence: This describes the experimental conditions and is supported by citations.

claim: A consistent amount of food was provided regardless of population size, which caused reproduction and survival to be density-dependent.
source: In both seasonal treatments, a consistent amount of food was provided regardless of population size, which caused reproduction and survival to be density-dependent (Betini et al., 2013a).
evidence: This describes the experimental design and its consequences, supported by a citation.

claim: Average mortality was reduced from 28% (±0.4) in the 'long-term control' populations to 0.5% (±1) in the 'stop selection' treatments.
source: Average mortality was reduced from 28% (±0.4; mean ± s.e.) in the 'long-term control' populations to 0.5% (±1) in these new 'stop selection' treatments.
evidence: This is a direct comparison of mortality rates between treatments.

claim: Mean thorax size after the non-breeding season was significantly lower than mean thorax size prior to the non-breeding season in high abundance conditions.
source: Mean thorax size after the non-breeding season was significantly lower than mean thorax size prior to the non-breeding season (Welch t-test: t = −2.87, df = 37.66, p=0.006), whereas there was no significant differences in average thorax in the low abundance treatment (Welch t-test: t = −0.55, df = 36.96, p=0.586; average size before = 1.318 mm; average size after the non-breeding season for the high abundance treatment was 1.225 and 1.297 mm for the low abundance treatment).
evidence: This is a result from an experimental validation of the body size measurement method.

claim: Population cycles can be inferred by investigating the shape of the estimated ACF where stationary periodic dynamics result in an oscillatory decay to zero of the ACF estimates.
source: Cycles can be inferred by investigating the shape of the estimated ACF: population cycles are characterized by stationary periodic dynamics, which result in an oscillatory decay to zero of the ACF estimates.
evidence: This describes the analytical method used to detect cycles.

claim: The positive correlation between body size and fecundity is well known in Drosophila.
source: In Drosophila, as in many other species, the positive correlation between body size and fecundity is well known (Mueller and Joshi, 2000; Appendix 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and reference to an appendix.

claim: Small individuals have higher survival during the non-breeding season when abundance is high in D. melanogaster.
source: and we previously demonstrated that small individuals have higher survival during the non-breeding season when abundance is high (Betini et al. 2013a, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.
